items.body:
There is a moment on "Tea Horse Road," the album's fourth track, where the saxophone drops to a near whisper and the percussion seems to breathe rather than strike. You realize you are not listening to two musicians from opposite sides of the world so much as two people who have agreed, without a word, on exactly how much silence costs.

Lao Dan grew up in Northeastern China near the North Korean border. He showed enough early talent on saxophone and bamboo flute to earn a place at conservatory, then walked away from it. He studied dizi formally in Beijing and later at Shenyang Conservatory before turning toward avant-garde jazz and free improvisation around 2013. What he took from that training was not obedience. It was control: a deep physical understanding of breath through a tube, and an instinct for space that most Western free players spend decades trying to locate.

Barcelona-based Vasco Trilla came to the drums late, at nineteen, through progressive rock and metal. He worked his way outward through jazz, African music, and free improvisation. He has since appeared on more than a hundred recordings for labels including NoBusiness, Clean Feed, and Cuneiform. He plays like a man who understands that the wrong note at the right moment is still the wrong note.

The seven tracks here, from the opener "You Are You" through the closing "Nobodies Are Going to Sleep," feel less like a set list than a field journal. Lao Dan moves between tenor saxophone and dizi (Chinese flute), changing not just tone but altitude. Trilla generates rhythm without always generating a pulse, which is a different and harder skill. On "Fire Boy," Dan's flute cuts upward in tight spirals while Trilla accelerates with the controlled intensity of someone who knows exactly how hot to let things get. "Tea Horse Road," named for the ancient trade route connecting Yunnan to Tibet, sits at the emotional center. It is patient, unresolved, and genuinely rooted. The drummer shakes what sounds like a string of small cymbals while giving Dan a wide, open background. As the piece heats up, the intensity feels both grounded and spiritually convincing.

The closing track thins out slowly until you are not sure whether you are still listening or simply sitting in the room where the music happened. It is a good place to leave things.

You Are You; New Species 1; New Species 2; Tea Horse Road; Old Heaven Books; Fire Boy; Nobodies Are Going to Sleep.

items.body:
In this recording by bassist, composer and bandleader Ben Wolfe, titled Any Time After Now, there is a quiet assurance, with nothing straining for effect or feeling manufactured. Recorded in a single studio day alongside vibraphonist Joel Ross, pianist Sullivan Fortner, tenor saxophonist Chris Lewis and drummer Aaron Kimmel, the album spans ten tracks of original Wolfe compositions and exhibits a natural cohesion that reflects musicians deeply attuned to one another.

The opener, "Any Time After Now," swings with effortless authority. Wolfe's bass lines move with confidence beneath Lewis and Ross's contributions, while Fortner brings a strong rhythmic sense to the tune. Kimmel takes an imaginative turn on his kit, adding to the bebop narrative. "Waltz II" is striking for its delicacy. Buoyed by Wolfe's deep tone and steady beat, Ross and Fortner interact with arresting sensitivity, each phrase answered by the other.

"Blues" evokes a hazy, after-hours atmosphere. Lewis delivers an expressive performance, smoky, relaxed, and soulful. Ross follows with an improvisation rich in harmonic nuance, and Fortner settles into a blues statement grounded in groove and touch. "5/4 Groove" unfolds as Kimmel shapes the asymmetrical pulse with ease, while Fortner crafts an extended meditation brimming with momentum and tension. Wolfe's solo is a highlight, lyrical, poised, and deeply musical.

Wolfe, an unusual musician who associates music with color, shape and texture, writes compositions that carry visual weight. The music shifts between shadows, light, density and openness with remarkable fluidity. The result is a performance in which the band knows exactly how to inhabit these spaces.

"Down with Gravity" brings sharp angles and earthy funk. Wolfe and Kimmel work hand in glove, while Lewis stretches out with a harmonic vocabulary that yields clarity of ideas. There is a real bite here without sacrificing sophistication. "Always Four" opens with an assertive flourish from Kimmel, then settles into tightly focused exchanges between Ross and Fortner. Kimmel is back on board with crisp playing, taking the tune out as each idea feels purposeful.

"Til The Next Time" is a silky bossa nova that glides effortlessly into the ear. Ross, in full vibrato, phrases beautifully over Wolfe's subtle plucking. Fortner and Kimmel keep everything light and pleasant. The closing bonus track, "Green," swings with optimism and zest. Ross and Fortner carry the instrumental load with a keen sense of musical drama, while Wolfe and Kimmel deliver sharply etched pulses. The number offers a clear picture of Wolfe's melodic, thoughtful, and generous compositional voice.

Any Time After Now; Waltz II; If Only; Blues; 5/4 Groove; Do You Love?; Down with Gravity; Always Four; 'Till Next Time; Green.

items.body:
Storybook: The Music Of Mark Miller is at one level the unfolding narrative of its 10 musical selections. At another, it is a tale about its primary author, Mark Miller, who traced his journey from {jny: Racine}} to New York City with his previous release Mark Miller: The Return Of Slide Huxtable (Slide Huxtable, 2008)—a long road that is a serious jazz player's dream of making it in the Big Apple. But most of all, it is a compelling reminder to listeners everywhere that the Manhattan jazz experience is incomplete without a trip to hear the Birdland Big Band.

Birdland's original, long defunct basement club at "The Jazz Corner of the World" (Broadway and 52nd) now occupies a bigger mid-town area, bounded on the north by Jazz at Lincoln Center (60 St.) and, on the south, by the "new" Birdland (44th St). Start at 52nd St., walk 8 blocks in either direction, and you are there. But which direction? Is there a significant difference? Some observers have suggested that big band music from the north references the genius of Duke Ellington, whereas the sounds to the south are aligned with the swing of Count Basie. Yet "Storybook," the eponymous title of the album's Grammy-nominated first track, sounds like something else entirely.

Miller—much of whose "schooling" was on the road as trombonist-composer with the Minneapolis-based jazz group, The Motion Poets—has constructed a brilliant sonic gateway that owes as much to Bach and Bartok as to Ellington or Count Basie. Starting with a stately 3-note descending motif, the composition builds on that figure with rich harmonies and vibrant dynamics, answered by an ascending counter-melody played by the lower brass. Soon, the entire sequence is repeated, with the addition of creative commentary from Brandon Lee's flugelhorn. After a sharply articulated, vigorously syncopated version of the primary motif, Kenny Barron's infectious "Water Lily." Unlike earlier recorded versions that are slower and light-spirited, the tune here is taken at a driving tempo with accompaniment by piano and drums that borders on the intrusive (likely due to an over-hot audio mix-down). Besides an inventive piano solo by Kenny Ascher, the piece showcases the commanding artistry of saxophonist Troy Roberts, whose closing cadenza balances impressive pyrotechnics with satisfying musical taste. Next, the standard, "Tenderly," lightens the mood with a sprightly version of a waltz that, with the notable exception of Bill Evans' up-tempo version, usually receives the slow, pensive reading of Rosemary Clooney or the even slower 4/4 versions by Sara Vaughn and Billie Holiday. Miller's arrangement exhibits remarkable attention to detail, replete with spiraling flutes that simulate butterflies to complement the spring setting for vocalist Nicole Zuraitis. Brief solos by Sam Dillon (a. sax) and Raul Agraz (trpt) fit seamlessly with the colorful seasonal mix.

Miller's own "Chorale and Alleluia" is as contemplative and celebratory as its title might suggest. It features the percussive thunder of Chris Smith, who will also be critical to the driving samba rhythm of Chick Corea's "Spain." Tom Harrell's "Sail Away" is an inviting melody launched without affectation by Glenn Drewes' reassuring flugel. After band director David DeJesus' soprano sax has taken control of the cruise, Drews resumes his storytelling by, in effect, shutting off the engine (i.e., piano, bass, drums) and allowing only the sounds of wind and water for several choruses—the pulse of the band sans rhythm section.

It is tempting to continue with a play-by-play analysis if only to identify the soloists in an ensemble with no weak links. The Birdland Band is "deep" with talent, each player capable of assuming solo duties on any given night. Take, for example, "WTF," in which trombonist/composer Miller resumes the cruise with a witty trombone exchange between James Burton III and Sara Jacovino, one that recalls the musical conversations by J.J. Johnson and Jay and Kai Winding.

The last third of the program is cued up by the standard "Close Your Eyes," which opens with Zuraitis close to the mic as she fashions a soft, pitch-perfect, improvised chorus before yielding to an Ascher piano solo that swings with the sure-fingered authority of Wynton Kelly. Following a good-humored, equally swinging turn by bass trombonist, James Borowski, Zuraitis re-enters for an "out" chorus that soon becomes "far-out," her voice rising in pitch and volume to the level of a Maynard Ferguson set-closer. It works because the vocalist implants herself in the trumpet section, rising to a powerful climax as the job requires. Finally, we receive a healthy reminder that "swing" does not require a thing except a ride cymbal and a hi-hat. (If only audio engineers could figure out a way to include the shimmer of a Zildjian in their mastering of live sounds.)

Rodrigo de Arunez's "Concierto" and Corea's "Spain" are worthy additions to those already in print. And they are among the most "honest," avoiding orchestral instruments (French horns, double reeds, tympani, etc.) as well as electronic devices (Fender Rhodes, phaser boxes, onboard modulating effects). The result is a focus that remains fixed on the music, not the gear. And then there is the memorable close-out for "Spain"—an ascending Miller bass-line that, in effect, resolves a sparking, fractious debate between big band and drums, then between sections within the ensemble.

"The DoubleDown," the last track of the regular program, evokes a Sunday night gospel meeting with its inviting singalong melody in ¾. The primary preacher is Ron Wilkins, whose testifying on plunger-muted trombone produces a meditative bass solo by Noriko Ueda. But rather than exit quietly, the congregation is led back by saxophones to the main theme, then a sudden stop and lift to a new key for a final testament by Mark Miller's emphatic postlude on trombone.

Church is out, but the congregation's spirits crave more action. "Nonsense," an original shuffle-rhythm blues composed by Miller and Zuraitis, answers the need to sustain the sense of play embedded in every true storybook. Zuraitis delivers a nonsensical lyric in the strongest musical terms, conversing over stop-time chords with Miller's and Wilkins' vocal trombones. Next, she handles "vocalese" lines in tight unison with tricky instrumental figures. Finally, there is a vocal exchange, over pedal-tone bass, between the entire band and its girl singer, who has the last word: "Nonsense? Come on, whatever gets you.

Small wonder that, after hearing a call like that, visitors are setting aside Friday nights for a return to Birdland.

Storybook; Water Lily; Tenderly; Chorale And Alleluia; Sail Away; WTF;; Close Your Eyes;; Concierto De Aranjuez; Spain; The Doubledown; Nonsense;.

items.body:
At a time when economics often dictates the size and scope of a jazz group, adding a guitarist to a typical piano-bass-drums trio makes a world of difference. And when said guitarist is Peter Bernstein, the difference is even more pronounced. That gives bassist Harvie S a clear headstart on Bright Dawn, a modest studio date with Bernstein broadening the usual trio setting on the bassist's 21st recording as leader of his own ensemble—the first, however, following a 15-year hiatus.

The other members of Harvie's group, each of whom plays a pivotal role, are pianist Miki Hayama (Fender Rhodes on "Ghosts of Havana" and "Voice in the Sky") and drummer Matt Wilson who introduces and sparks the perky "I've Got Rhythm and Blues." That is one of Harvie's eight compositions, escorting Bob Dorough's playful "Devil May Care" and Chick Corea's sunny "Humpty Dumpty."

And therein lies the session's most problematic aspect. Even though decent and well-intentioned, Harvie's compositions are, to be frank, several lengthy strides away from memorable. While that may be traced in part to the group's makeup and Harvie S's resolve to lead the way, the fact remains that the success of any collective enterprise, regardless of size or shape, rests in large measure on its choice of material, and most of the songs on Bright Dawn simply don't measure up, even with Bernstein on board to help enliven them.

Harvie must be given props for naming one of his themes "Navalny" (and enhancing it with arco and string bass) but even that melody seems tame when compared to what comes next, the spunky "Rhythm and Blues," one of the session's few high spots. Hayama is an impressive soloist, as is Bernstein, and their expertise must be noted. That is not, however, nearly enough to raise Bright Dawn above the norm.

Ghosts of Havana; Devil May Care; Waltz for Vartan; Navalny; I've Got Rhythm and Blues; Yukimi's Song; Humpty Dumpty; The Truth; Voice in the Sky; Swithering.

Are perfumes composed? Do they evolve? Polish-Canadian trumpeter and composer Jacques Kuba Séguin says they do, emphatically, with his La Trilogie des Odeurs: Three Works, Three Universes, One Story.

In presenting an olfactory world via an auditory work of art, there is a sense that Séguin is taking things well beyond just perfume to an entire world of odors. It also suggests an entanglement of the senses, and Séguin pushes this suggestion to the max with this trilogy in three separate albums.
items.body:
Are perfumes composed? Do they evolve? Polish-Canadian trumpeter and composer Jacques Kuba Séguin says they do, emphatically, with his La Trilogie des Odeurs: Three Works, Three Universes, One Story.

In presenting an olfactory world via an auditory work of art, there is a sense that Séguin is taking things well beyond just perfume to an entire world of odors. It also suggests an entanglement of the senses, and Séguin pushes this suggestion to the max with this trilogy in three separate albums. For Parfum no. 1, he convenes a jazz quartet with pianist Jean-Michel Pilc, bassist Rémi-Jean Leblanc, drummer Kevin Warren, with vocalist Elizabeth Shepherd sitting in on one tune. Leave the connection of odor to sound to the listener here. Synesthesia—where the stimulation of one sense triggers experiences in another—is a real thing. Pianist Jessica Williams said she saw colors with every note or chord she played.

Of the three Parfum albums, No. 1, 2 and 3, Parfum no. 1 is the starkest—a spare, dry sound that may evoke the smell of desert sage as it rides the Santa Ana winds through the chaparral, picking up molecules of the menthol eucalyptus that flourishes in the riverbeds, the rich aromas of damp earth from which these craggy apparitions writhe.

There is much space here, like that desert landscape that birthed the sage. Melodic simplicity and repetition make the music sound ritualistic in a beautiful way. Elizabeth Shepherd's vocals (invocations?) in French are hushed whisperings on "Je suis là."

The music is expressed with an understated patience, as it was in Miles Davis' Ascenseur pour l'échafaud (Fontana, 1957). It is an inward sound that invites reflection and contemplation.

The three albums as a whole are described as a trilogy of smells celebrating the olfactory memories of our lives. This, in itself, marks out ambitious territory via three distinct albums—Parfum no. 1 utilizing the jazz quartet; Parfum no 2 employing a 17-piece jazz band; and Parfum no. 3 bringing in a symphony orchestra, taking the ambitious aspect off the charts.

The olfactory experiences described, auditorily, on Parfum no. 1 are subtle, whiffs of mixed fragrances. Parfum no. 2, the big band set, brings in a riot of bright smells, with brassy primary colors underlain by understated pastel scents and rainbow swirls of harmonic whirlpoolings. Scents and sounds, with their ability to appeal to ephemeral memories in the subconscious yet formative aspects of our life histories, emerge through open-ear listening.

The final chapter, Parfum no. 3 enfolds the jazz quartet with L'Orchestre Symphonique de Trois-Rivières, led by Alain Trudel. Séguin speaks of: "Base notes, or earth notes...the essence of the perfume, the part that clings to the skin and remains imprinted in objects as well as in the soul." While the first chapter of this trilogy speaks to a simplicity of expression and the elementary, youthful experience of the fragrance, Parfum no. 3 takes that early introduction into the complexities of understanding born of time and wisdom into a richer and more complex landscape. It is an illuminating listening experience, seven compositions that intertwine and respond to each other with the angelic symphonic wings of the orchestra.

CD 1: La danse du hasard; Promesse de souvenirs; Rencontre au berceau; Je suis là; Éphémère; Candeur. CD 2: La danse du hasard et des dangers; 26 printemps; Paysage pour Muniak; 40 is the new 30; Gratitude. CD 3: How we start again; Il n'y a pas de hasard; Fugue avec Anaïs (à Métis); Entre l'exil et l'insomnie - partie I L'exil; In coelum; Entre l'exil et l'insomnie - partie II L'insomnie; le cortège des fragrances - Les aléas de Mme P.

items.body:
Rightfully described as a thinking (wo)man's jazz musician, trumpeter-composer-bandleader Steven Bernstein makes deeply cerebral music no matter whether with his own ensembles such as Sexmob and Millennial Territory Orchestra or in heady collaborations with other artists such Jacob Fred Jazz Odyssey (see Race Riot Suite (Royal Potato Family, 2011)).

In fact, the products of his imagination resound with such visceral force that those creations render an impact comparable to his membership in Levon Helm's Midnight Ramble Band (or MTO's tribute to Sly Stone). ResoNation Trio and Ultra Resonance, are similarly charged, the former a forward-thinking yet traditionalist-leaning project for which Bernstein recruited the estimable rhythm section of bassist Scott Colley and drummer Nasheet Waits, the latter is a reimagining of that threesome's music overseen by pedigreed engineer and producer Scotty Hard (a long-time collaborator of visionaries unto themselves, Medeski Martin & Wood).

The former is as skeletal as the latter is dense. Yet the two recordings, distinctly different in concept and execution, are nevertheless inextricably linked. Each, in its own way, is a thought-provoking piece, with the respective virtues redolent when played separately or together in sequence, either in the configuration of the single CD or the double vinyl package.

The abstract likes of Bernstein-Colley-Waits' "Turf" benefit as much from the space in the arrangement as the linear progression the three pursue in "Pettiford." Meanwhile, corresponding titles of the companion piece, such as "Rubidium," function similarly, gateways into more or less otherworldly realms (though perhaps not as mesmerizing as the source of that concept, dub reggae recordings by Burning Spear on Garvey's Ghost (Island Records, 1976)).

It is not necessary to listen to Ultra Resonance on headphones to appreciate its aura. Still, that method can reveal more of the multiple layers in the recordings. And, in its own way, that method also proves to be comparatively applicable to the acoustic music: the patient and probing human three-way human interactions that comprise "Woodstock," for instance, radiate both the physical and mental effort involved in the musicianship.

Hard's deeply insistent reformulation of the music through the use of keyboards, various other instruments and percussion, in combination with Jeremy Gustin's varied rhythm devices, emits a presence as haunting as that in the spacious interplay of the ResoNation Trio. Selections from the latter like the one non-original, the blues of "Sitting On Top of the World," resound with comparable levels of mental acumen infused with technical expertise.

A comparatively spooky atmosphere thus pervades most of this seventy-six minutes, even as it is presented in cuts of mostly 3 to 5 minute duration. With its infectious lively cheer, the penultimate track by the trumpeter, bassist and drummer, titled "South," may be the exception to the rule. And the product of Scotty Hard's efforts, such as "Vibranium," are like nothing so much as an individual's inner monologue, filtered through devices, as are so many of our contemporary dialogues.  On the other hand, the acoustic portion effectively constitutes a friendly but lively debate between equals.

Accordingly, the sounds from the three-man ensemble flicker in and out of the well-defined, but dark audio mix during "Argon." And, without ever going on too long to become monotonous, there are just enough similar turns of melody to render more pronounced the heavily rhythmic likes of "Titano." In the end, the overall pacing is that of a well-sequenced live set, without an overabundance of aural esoterica.

It is thus indicative of the seamless yet malleable nature of ResoNation Trio and Ultra Resonance that various elements from each can be interwoven with the other. Reprogramming the CD tracks or alternating the four sides of vinyl extends both the accessibility and the durability of Steven Bernstein and company's eccentric musical orthodoxy.

Turf; Pettiford; Two Shakes; Woodstock; August 3; West; Mammoth; Question; South; Sitting on Top of the World; Argon; Erbium; Chromium; Vibranium; Rubidium; Titano; Radon; Niobium.

items.body:
Larry McCray's Heartbreak City, released on Keeping the Blues Alive Records, is steeped in grit, anguish, resilience and hard-won joy. The album reflects the life of a working-class blues man who sharpened his craft in the clubs of Saginaw after shifts on the General Motors assembly line, before touring nationally and eventually across Europe with Albert Collins. Every track carries the emotional weight of decades spent earning success the hard way, drawing deeply from McCray's Arkansas roots while sounding fully grounded in the modern blues tradition.

"Try to Be a Good Man," co-written by McCray, serves as both introduction and mission statement. Riding a chugging roadhouse groove—with a bright, punctuating all-star horn section featuring Dan Fornero, Wayne Bergeron, Andy Martin and Sal Lozano—the song doubles as advice for younger men navigating relationships. McCray's baritone, earthy, warm and unforced, anchors lines such as: "Give her all the love you can and do your best to understand." His guitar work is concise and expressive, delivering sharp, brittle, conversational bends that echo the influence of Little Milton without slipping into imitation. The performance highlights one of McCray's defining strengths: emotional honesty delivered without theatrics.

The title track provides the album's emotional center. Built on a deep blues-rock pocket shaped by the modern production style associated with producers Joe Bonamassa and Josh Smith, "Heartbreak City" unfolds with the restless momentum of an open highway. McCray's stinging guitar lines recall Albert King, while his vocal phrasing again nods to Milton. The song captures the album's defining theme: a man worn down by loss, disappointment and the daily grind, yet still unwilling to surrender. It is weary and determined at the same time, balancing vulnerability with quiet resolve.

On "Everything Falls on Me," McCray channels his frustration through a mid-tempo blues-rock groove shaped by Bo Diddley-style syncopation and terse, declarative guitar figures reminiscent of Chuck Berry. Its lyrics about carrying everyone else's burdens strike a familiar chord without lapsing into self-pity. "When it comes to disaster, Red Cross got nothin' on me / I've cleaned up more messes than the human eye can see / Be it friend or family or someone I just met / They only hit me up for something, anything they can get." McCray sings with a convincing authority that transforms everyday frustrations into something universal.

McCray's songwriting strengths surface again in "Bye Bye Blues," co-written with Charlie Walmsley and nominated for Song of the Year at the 2026 Blues Music Awards. Built around the line, "When I said hello to you, I said goodbye to the blues," the song balances classic blues sentiment with understated optimism and demonstrates McCray's ability to write memorable, emotionally direct material.

Throughout Heartbreak City, McCray honors the artists who shaped him while remaining unmistakably himself. Positioned somewhere between Albert King's fire and Little Milton's silky soulfulness, he delivers performances defined by warmth, grit and emotional clarity. In an era still searching for towering modern blues voices, McCray makes a compelling case for his place near the top of the genre's current generation.

Try To Be A Good Man; Heartbreak City; Bye Bye Blues; Bright Side; Everything Falls On Me; I Know What I Have Done; Keep On Loving My Baby; Hangman; Stop Your Crying; Crazy World.

items.excerpt:
Evidence lives up to its title very well. A lot of music in this fairly short album that makes itself heard with surprising simplicity.

items.body:
Evidence lives up to its title very well. A lot of music in this fairly short album that makes itself heard with surprising simplicity.

EVIDENCE is a quartet: reeds, trombone, cello and drums. An unusual formation, but one that recalls Henry Threadgill's Zooid from 2015 onwards (without the guitar): In For A Penny, In For A Pound (Pi Recordings, 2015) and Poof. Sol Léna-Schroll (alto saxophone and clarinet) is Threadgill, Jørgen Bjelkerud (trombone) is Jose Davila, Joel Ring that of Christopher Hoffman, and Trym Saugstad Karlsen (drums) is Elliot Humberto Kavee.

The comparison goes no further. For here the music takes flight. The absence of piano and bass is turned to advantage in airy compositions and improvisations, whereas with Threadgill, drums and tuba (which Davila also plays) often take it upon themselves to bring everyone back down to earth. It is a feat of Karlsen's to breathe pulses that propel the music into the air.

Léna-Schroll and Bjelkerud are fellow members of Orchestra for Jazz Composers in Oslo / Orkesteret for Jazzkomponister Oslo (OJKOS) and L'Autre Collectif/Det Andre Kollektivet, a compelling initiative funded by France and Norway since 2019, where the innovative aspects of jazz and sometimes contemporary music are explored, and from which the label Autres Records was born. Bjelkerud and Karlsen appear in Amalie Dahl's Dafnie EXTENDED Live at Moldejazz, Ring in Eon, from Karoline Wallace's quintet, and Karlsen in The Aftermath (Fjordgata Records, 2026), of the major Ingeborg Gravem Sollid quartet, all almost simultaneously released. We are, in other words, at the very top of the tree.

The compositions and arrangements are precise and tightly structured. From them emerge improvisations in which the saxophone and trombone interlock in virtuosic spirals ("Mad Blue"). Freed from any earthly support, improvisation breaks free harmonically from the theme, while maintaining its formal rigour.

The brisk compositions would readily be described as bop in other circumstances, with perhaps a welcome Braxtonian touch. In particular, Léna-Schroll delivers a highly inspired solo in "Infinite Loop." The quieter pieces showcase the timbral contrasts, exemplified by an exquisite dialogue between Ring and Bjelkerud in "Infinite Fase."

This is an album of very high calibre with a great deal of substance. The lively and more measured pieces follow one another in a way that gives the album a fine balance. This beautiful, intelligent album is a breath of fresh air, an invitation to freedom, the opening of morning windows, and a day filled with positive energy.

Mad Blue; Infinite Down (#3); Band Music; Choral; Infinite Loop (#1); Infinite Fase (#2).

items.body:
The fourteen-member Hot House West Swing Orchestra, enabled by Salt Lake City, Utah's nonprofit Hot House West, makes its recorded debut with Joy in Rhythm, Vol. 1, an array of eleven danceable songs, most of which were popular during the Swing Era's golden age in the 1930s and '40s.

This is an album especially designed for dancing; it even includes a booklet that teaches the listener a number of simple dance moves tailored for beginners. In spite of the fact that there are several cursory solos along the way (the longest by violinist Curtis Woodbury), this is not a jazz album per se but one that borrows the rhythms of jazz—most notably swing—to press home its danceable message.

As a guide for dancers, Joy in Rhythm works fairly well. One can imagine a dance floor filled with men and women who are grooving to the music. Remove dancing from the equation, however, and the album reveals a number of flaws, not the least of which is the many liberties taken with the character and tempo of the original compositions—some or even all of which were no doubt deemed necessary to make the finished product more accessible to dancers.

The orchestra's vocalists, Hayley Kirkland and Nathan Royal (who doubles on lead guitar and whistling), are at least on a par with many Swing Era band singers, which can be taken as rather faint praise. As for the orchestra, in terms of power and consonance, it is somewhere below the norm when compared to working professional ensembles, which the Hot House West orchestra does not claim to be. To verify that impression, one need do no more than listen to the closing number, Count Basie's classic "One O'Clock Jump." Case closed.

As no one is likely to amass much wealth performing with this group, it is assuredly a labor of love. And that is perhaps how it should be appraised—as a heartfelt summons to dancers and would-be dancers to leave the couch, head for a ballroom and immerse themselves in the irrepressible Joy of Rhythm.

Dark Eyes; Honeysuckle Rose; I'm Gonna Sit Right Down (And Write Myself a Letter); On the Sunny Side of the Street; Katusha; Grand Terrace Rhythm; I've Got Spurs (That Jingle, Jangle, Jingle); Hit That Jive Jack; A Mellow Bit of Rhythm; Them There Eyes; One O'clock Jump
